course.title: Acute bowel obstructions
course.html:
= Abnormal persistent suppression of effective bowel movements with local, regional and general consequences

  • pluri-etiologic/ pluri-pathogenic

Classifications

  • a) Topographic
  • Upper/ High
  • Lower/ Low
  • b) Pathogenic
  • Vascular involvement
  • Prognosis decided by presence/ absence of ischemia

Etiology

  • 1. Adhesions (40%) -> post-OP
  • 2. Malignant (cancer) obstructions (20%)
  • 3. External strangulations (15%)
  • 4. Early post-OP (6.8%)
  • 5. Mesenteric vascular occlusion (6.5%)
  • 6. Volvulus (5%)
  • 7. Benign obstructive tumors (3%)
  • 8. Obturator obstructions (2%)
  • 9. Internal hernias (0.5%)
  • 10. Invaginations
Obstructive
(mechanical obstruction)		- Complete or incomplete (subacute) obstruction
- Without affecting, at least initially, blood supply of intestinal wall
A. Extrinsic compressions
I. Tumors (benign/ malignant)
- Mesenterial, uterus, ovary, liver
- Retroperitoneal (primary, kidney, adrenal, pancreas)
- Lymph nodes
II. Adhesions (visceral, parietal)
III. Foreign bodies (left after surgery)
B. Intramural lesions
I. Congenital stenoses
II. Tumors (benign, malignant, primary, metastases)
III. Inflammatory stenoses (specific: TBC, CD; non-specific: postradiation, scars)
IV. Intramural hematomas
C. Endoluminal obstacles
- Gallstones (biliary ileus)
- Food bolus (Phytobezoars)
- Hair bolus (Trichobezoars)
- Worms (Ascariasis, Ascarid ball)
- Accidental (tooth fragments, bones, wood, plastic) -> pylorus, duodenal
curvatures, ileo-cecal valve, rectosigmoid flexure, anal canal
Strangulations- Obstruction of bowel (“double closed loop”, “one end” closed loop) with
interruption of venous/arterial supply -> ischemia, necrosis and perforation
A. External
- Hernias
- Incisional hernias
- Eviscerations
B. Internal
- Internal hernias
- Invaginations (intussusceptions)
- Volvulus
- Obstructing/ strangulating – ischemic adhesion
Vascular (bowel infarctions)- By far most severe variant, with highest mortality !
A. Acute arterial obstruction
- Embolus, thromb-embolus
B. Acute venous obstruction
C. Acute microcirculation obstruction
Functional
(non-mechanical/
Paralytic ileus)		- Occur at segmental level or entire length of intestinal tract
- Produced by exaggerated, prolonged spasms -> bowel paresis (adynamic ileus)
- Absence of any mechanical obstruction with intact intestinal vascularization
A. Metabolic causes
- Severe acidosis (diabetes mellitus, “status asthmaticus”), uremia, severe
electrolyte imbalances (hypopotassemia, hyponatremia), hypothyroidism,
hypoproteinemia
- Severe anemias
- Abdominal (pelvic) irradiation
- Neurologic lesions: epilepsy, brain tumors, MS, colon pseudo-obstruction
B. Reflex causes
- Post-operative bowel paresis
- Mesenterial torsion / cavitary organs distension
- fallopian tube torsion
- reno-ureteral colic
- biliary colic
- acute urinary bladder distension
- Thoracic disorders (pneumonia, thoracic traumas, myocardial infarction – bowel
paresis associated with epigastric pain and shock ! )
- Retroperitoneal disorders (hematomas, acute pancreatitis, abscesses)
- Sterile intraperitoneal fluid collections
- acute onset of ascites in liver cirrhosis
- hemoperitoneum
- chemical peritonitis
C. Septic causes
- Localized/ diffuse peritonitis
- Septic conditions adjacent to peritoneal serosa (pelvic, retroperitoneal abscess)
  • double closed loops (volvulus, strangulations)

Pathophysiology

  • → 3 major initial events

a. Motility ceases b. Obstruction of bowel c. Obstruction of vascular

  • → 4 main types
  • 1. Functional (a)
  • 2. Obstructive (b)
  • 3. Strangulated (b+c)
  • 4. Vascular (c)
  • Alterations of homeostasis initially start at affected loop and of intestinal tract upstream
  • At onset -> noxious stimulus due to increased intralumenal tension -> increase in peristaltism and excessive enteral gland secretion
  • Peristaltic fight followed by energy exhaustion of muscle fibers -> onset of distension and inability to reabsorb fluids -> endolumenal accumulation of fluids and gas => huge atonic upstream bowl reservoir containing enormous fluid and gas accumulations
  • Fluids come from: saliva, gastric juice, biliary fluid, pancreatic juice, enteral juice
  • Results in severely dehydrated (3rd space fluid loss) and electrolyte imbalance
  • Gas accumulations from swallowed air, biochemical reactions and activity of microbial flora
  • Increased intestinal distension -> pressure increases -> bowel wall squashed -> venous circulation closed
    • > eventually capillary collapse -> wall edema -> ischemia and necrosis (irreversible)
  • Ascites common (another third compartment)
  • Mixed (metabolic and respiratory) acidosis
  • Obstruction by strangulation -> necrosis is specific -> closely followed by infection and toxaemia
    • > rapidly septico-toxic and/ or hypovolemic shock

Clinical manifestation

  • Pain: colicy, intermitent pain, rapid increase in intensity (max. of 30-60s) followed by rapid and total decrease
  • Initially located at level of obstruction and subsequently becomes generalized
  • Pain free time interval between colics has clinical relevance
  • Obstruction in proximal jejunal - 5 min, ileum - 5-20 min, colon more - > 20 min.
  • Strangulations and enteromesenteric infarctions - permanent, high intensity pain, cannot be controlled by pain killers
  • Volvulus – rapid, complete, brutal, syncopal onset, with same continuous high intensity pain
  • Paralytic ileus - pain diffuse, continuous, low-moderate intensity
  • Vomiting: initially reflex (pain, distension), later becomes effortless, abundant and productive with regurgitation, due to antiperistaltic waves and “overfullness
  • Brings no relieve to patient !
  • High, proximal obstructions - vomiting is early, repeated, persistent, clear biliary fluid
  • Low ileal obstructions - initial containes food remains, then becomes bilious, later porraceous (turbid bile) and finally fecaloid (false fecal vomiting)
  • Low, distal (recto-sigmoid) - occurs late and is less common
  • Faeculent vomit = sign of severity, due to abnormal overgrow of faecal bacteria at 24-48 hours after onset
  • Absence of fecal and gas transit (obstipation)
  • In high obstructions, initial passage from distal intestine possible (dangerous delay of diagnosis)
  • Subocclusive (König) syndrome = characteristic for incomplete obstructions of small intestine and ileocecal segment -> colicy pain at fixed point (level of obstruction), increased meteorism, hydro-aeric noises, borborgym, finally diarrhea and gas passage (relief); similar episodes reoccur
  • Bloody-glaireous stools in some invaginations and enteromesenteric infarction (late clinical sign – severe prognosis !)

Physical examination

Abdominal signs

Inspection

  • Meteorism is characteristic, occur during first 24 hours, abdominal distension
  • Functional ileus - distension is intense and diffuse, yet painless
  • Mechanical obstructions of distal ileum - distension in center of abdomen
  • Distal rectosigmoid obstructions - meteorism is extensive, but localized in flanks and epigastric
  • Sigmoid volvulus - most extensive abdominal distension, asymmetrical, ovoid, oriented from left iliac fossa towards right upper quadrant
  • Small bowel volvulus - central and asymmetrical balloon
  • Abdominal distension absent in extremely high occlusions, Richter type hernias, early phases of all bowel obstructions
  • Visible peristaltism at abdominal wall in lean patients with mechanical obstruction
  • If constant location and fixed point -> König syndrome
  • Also detect postoperative scars, external hernias

Palpation

  • Migrating tumor masses – invaginations and faecalomas, fixed tumor masses (stenosing tumors)
  • Inflamatory tumors
  • Localized areas of tenderness and/or rigidity in ischaemic obstructions (strangulations, torsions, intussusceptions, infarctions)

Percussion

  • Tympanism that covers hepatic dullness
  • Meteorism
  • Localized dullness in case of loops filled with liquid
  • Shifting dullness in ascites

Auscultation

  • Hydro-aeric bowel sounds and borborygmi
  • In functional bowel pareses - “abdominal quiet”
  • “death silence” in bowel infarctions

Rectal exam

  • Compulsory
  • Empty rectal ampulla (Hochwag sign)

Extra-abdominal signs

  • Initially, normal pulse, no fever, only anxiety, tachycardia during colicky episodes
  • Eventually, general condition progressively alters, finally occlusive septic-toxic shock
  • “tormented” facies by ischemic colic or strangulation
  • Signs of severe dehydration (thirst, dry tongue, hypotonic eye globes, persistent flaccid cutaneous fold) + decreased diuresis (empty urinary bladder at initial catheterisation)
  • Fever - infected necrosis or diffuse peritonitis
  • Marmoreal skin, hemodynamic collapse and hypothermia - late, terminal phases of septico-toxic shock

Paraclinical examination

  • Plain abdominal radiography - most valuable, gas-fluid levels 4-6 hours of onset
    • Functional bowel paresis - hydro-aeric images uniformly distributed, from stomach to whole intestine (“chessboard” images)
    • Small bowel obstructions - hydro-aeric images numerous, in central abdominal area, large transverse diameter
    • Distal colic - gas-fluid levels less numerous, outline colic frame, large vertical diameter
  • Irrigography – nowadays not used routinely
  • Abdominal ultrasound - routine techniques, degree of loop distension, wall thickness, presence of peristaltism, fluid in peritoneal cavity, etiology of occlusive syndrome
  • Abdominal CT - most valuable technique, establish underlying cause
  • Mesenteric angiography/Angio MRI - extremely useful although rarely used, determine site of vascular obstructions in ischemia
  • Endoscopy - less frequently in emergency, detect duodenal obstructions
  • Laparoscopy - extremely useful for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, care must be taken to prevent iatrogenic bowel’s lesions due to meteorism

Differential diagnosis

  • Chest trauma, pneumonia, basal pleurisy, right ventricle myocardial infarction
  • Acute adynamic bowel distension in severe, prolonged bronchial asthma episodes (“status astmaticus”) - characterized by continuous anal gas emission (not by failure to pass flatus !)
  • Acute gastric distension (usually postoperative) subsides on application of nasogastric suction tube
  • Acute ascites after hepatic portal decompensation
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Painful subumbilical “tumor” - important urinary bladder distention
  • Neglected diffuse peritonitis
  • Psychogenic distension in “ghost pregnancy”

Clinical variant

  • Proximal small bowel obstructions
    • Sudden onset, rapid evolution
    • Early, frequent, profuse vomiting
    • Rapidly and highly unbalancing fluid-ion losses -> hypovolemic shock
    • Abdominal distension initially absent (“flat abdomen”)
    • Gas and stools emissions spontaneously or by enema
  • Distal ileal obstructions
    • Slower evolution
    • Third compartment extremely extensive
    • Vomiting occurs later, abundant, turbid, later faeculent
    • Colicky episodes less frequent, every 15-20 minutes
    • Abdominal distension symmetrical, central
    • Dehydration occurs later but is severe
  • Low (recto-sigmoid) obstructions
    • Long progressive, well tolerated evolution ove several days (4-7 days)
    • Less intense colicky episodes, intervals > 20 minutes
    • Vomiting absent or late
    • Important abdominal distension (flanks and epigastric, later generalized)
    • Rectal digital examination frequently detect cause
    • Majority caused by malignant tumors (aged patients, multiple comorbidities)
    • Diastatic perforations -> severe faecaliod diffuse peritonitis with very high mortality rates
      • ➔Repeated abdominal X-ray examinations for early detection of cecal distension close to 12- 13c m (“critical cecal diameter”)
    • Colic perforations just above obstructive tumor (extended necrosis of obstructed colon)
  • Volvulus
    • Rotation (torsion) of bowel loop by > 180° with “double closed loop” ->interruption of circulation
    • Sudden onset, continuous (not intermittent-colicky !), very intense pain; vomiting
    • Abdominal distension - central, symmetrical in jejunal volvulus; lower, asymmetrical, left iliac fossa to right upper quadrant in sigmoid volvulus
    • Due to full, heavy, long, mobile and hyperperistaltic loops, posterior parietal insertion points are fixed and close to one another
    • Mortality high
  • Intestinal intussusceptions (invaginations)
    • Frequent in children
    • Sudden onset with typical intermittent colic, with longer periods of calmness
    • Rectal bleeding in 25%
    • “migrating tumor” can be detected by palpation only in 20% of cases
    • Metorism at late stage
    • Can be chronic recurring
    • Venous circulation (later arterial too !) blocked
    • After 48 hours adhesions between invaginated cylinders already tight -> irreversible -> ischemia and necrosis
    • Usually triggered by inestinal tumor (adenomatous polyps, diverticula, foreign bodies) (triggering enteral tumors are mostly benign, colic tumors are malignant !)
    • Can be entero-enteral, ileo-colic, ileo-cecal, colo-colic
  • Internal hernias
    • Entrapment of mobile loops in orifices, recesses, pouches within peritoneal cavity with or without strangulation
    • Aquired (abdominal-or thoracic trauma, surgery) or congenital
    • Internal hernias in preexisting orifices and fossettes
      • ➔paraduodenal hernias
      • ➔paracecal (Rieux) hernias
      • ➔hernias through foramen of Winslow (Treitz)
      • ➔congenital diaphragmatic hernias
    • Internal hernias through traumatically or iatrogenically generated orifices
      • ➔diaphragmatic
      • ➔transmesocolic (after gastrojejnostomies, Roux en Y loop, etc.)
      • ➔transmesenteric (retro-anastomotic after gastro-jejunal tube placement)
    • Mortality rates high
  • Strangulated external hernias
    • Strangulated intestinal content (double closed loop) initiating ischemic necrosis
    • Violent (abrupt onset of intense, continuous pain at strangulation, vomiting, pallor, sweating)
    • Examination promptly detects strangulation -> diagnosis established early
    • Femoral hernias have highest risk of strangulation, but inguinal hernias more frequent
    • Femoral hernias with lateral (incomplete) strangulation do not cause intestinal occlusion, but manifest by diarrhea (resulting in dangerous delay in diagnosis and treatment !)
  • Incisional hernias
    • With or without strangulation
    • Intrasaccular adhesions or at level of fibrotic hernial rings

Treatment

  • Main therapeutic targets
    • Restoration of water-ion and acid-base balance
    • Relieve gastrointestinal distension
    • Treat cause of enterocolic obstruction
    • Prevent future episodes
  • Preoperative preparation
    • Placement of naso-gastric suction tube (evacuation of gastrointestinal content, suppression of vomiting, relieving of distension, breaking vicious circle between distension and wall ischemia; no aspiration, allows general anaesthesia, no fluid and ion loss)
    • 2 large iv lines or CVC -> fluids and rebalance (the longer the obstrusction, the more time it takes for re-equilibrium and until surgery can be performed) + monitoring of CVP
    • Placing urinary catheter (evaluation of rehydration)
    • Large spectrum antibiotics
    • Alpha/ beta blocker or preferably, continuous epidural catheter -> opening of intestinal microcirculation
    • Pain killers
  • Surgical treatment
    • 2 major objectives: removal of obstruction and removal of toxic intestinal content and peritoneal effusions
    • Timing of operation chosen depending on type of obstruction (ischemic or non-ischemic); duration of evolution; coexistence of associated diseases
    • Immediate emergency surgery in
      • ➔All types of bowel strangulations
      • ➔Acute colic obstructions with “critical cecal diameter”
      • ➔All small bowel obstructions hospitalized before severe water-ion imbalances
      • ➔Any occlusive variant with ischemia
    • Delayed surgery to do re-equilibration
      • ➔Mechanical non-ischaemic obstruction with water-ion imbalances
      • ➔Severe concomitant life-threatening visceral failures
    • Approach route - median sub- and supra-umbilical laparotomy
    • Criteria for assessment of viability of loop: color of loop, peristaltism, arterial pulsations
    • If loop not viable -> resection compulsory with/ without restoration of digestive tract continuity
    • If loops viable -> decompression of digestive tract with evacuation of toxic-septic content
      • ➔“retrograde milking” up to level of naso-gastric or large suction tube
      • ➔decompression of colon by thick transanal Faucher tubes
      • ➔decompression by opening digestive tract
    • In small bowel obstruction - dividing adhesions; devolvulation; disinvagination,; release from internal/ external hernias; enterotomy with extraction of calculus/ foreign body with enterorrhaphy; excision of tumors (uterine, mesenteric tumors); segmental resection in inflammatory/ malignant stenoses
    • In resectable colorectal tumors -> “all-in-one” strategy = resection of lesion + anastomosis
    • In irresectable colorectal tumors -> internal by-pass
      • ➔ileo-transversostomy - in cecal, ascending colon or right flexure obstructive neoplasms
      • ➔transverso-transversostomy - in mid transverse colon obstructions
      • ➔transverso-sigmoidostomy - in splenic flexure malignant stenoses
      • ➔external diversions (permanent or temporary enterostomies, colostomies -> radical resection accomplished 2-3 weeks later if possible with concomitant reconstruction
  • Postoperative treatment
    • Maintenance of nasogastric suction until resumption of digestive transit
    • Volemic, ion and acid-base re-equilibration continued
    • Antibiotherapy
    • Symptomatic treatment (pain killers, ...)
  • Functional occlusions (paralytic ileus)
    • First intent is to find cause and treat it
    • Post-OP transit should re-occur after 72 h
    • Conservative treatment usually enough
    • Surgery only for underlying cause (e.g, appendicitis, peritonitis) or complications (e.g., perforation)
    • Initial bowl rest
    • IV fluids, analgesics
    • Nasogastric suction tube (not always neccessary)
    • Stimulation of intestinal transit
      • ➔Continuous peridural infiltration
      • ➔Laxatives or prokinetics
      • ➔Early initiation of enteral feeding if tolerated
      • ➔Mobilisation as soon as possible

Complications

  • Untreated development
  • Necroses
  • Diastatic caecal perforations
  • Diffuse/ localized peritonitis
  • Septico-toxic shock with multiple organ failures
  • Pre- and intraoperative complications
  • Gastric/ intestinal content aspiration -> severe bronchopneumonia
  • Bowel perforations -> peritonitis
  • Postoperative complications
  • Eviscerations
  • ARDS
  • Acute cardiac, respiratory, renal, hepatic failures
  • Acute stress digestive lesions (UDH)
  • Pulmonary thrombembolism
  • Acute gastric dilation
  • Anastomotic fistulae, abdominal abcesses, peritonitis, sepsis
  • Multiple recurrent obstructive episodes
  • Blind loop syndrome (consequence of internal diversions that exclude large, extended bowel segments)
  • Short bowel syndrome (after extended bowel resections)

Obstructions

  • → SHOCK!!!
  • Critical fluid loss (9%)
  • Hypersecretion + absorption ceased
  • 3rd parasytic hydric compartment
  • 1. Fluid/ electrolyte redistribution
  • 2. Septicity (bact. translocation)

Metabolic acidosis

  • 1. Predominant alkaline loss
  • 2. Cellular catabolism
  • 3. Respiratory acidosis

Intraenteric pressure (normal 1.4-2.8 mmHg)

  • Arterioles 30-35 mmHg
  • Capillaries 15 mmHg
  • → Venules 10mmHg!
  • → Double closed loop → 45 mmHg

Strangulations

  • → Necrosis and sepsis
  • Viability of bowel early compromised
    • Requires immediate emergency surgery
    • Clinical features are alarming

Signs and symptoms

  • Pain: acute, continuous, sudden
  • Vomiting
  • Abdominal distension: early
  • Constipation
  • Anxious, pale, tachycardic, sweating, tendency to shock
  • Abdomen is painful on palpation, localized muscle defense

Radiology

  • Plain X-ray
  • CT

DD

  • 1. Acute gastric distension
  • 2. Acute obstruction of urinary bladder
  • 3. Acute ascites
  • 4. Pregnancy/ dyspepsia
  • 5. Asthma
  • 6. Chronic constipation (fecaloma)
  • 7. ABOS + SHOCK (acute pancreatitis, mesenteric infarction, acute MI)

Treatment

Pre-OP= 1-3 → 12h
1. CVC (ZVK)
2. 2 PVC’s
3. Nasogastric tube (NGST)
4. +/- epidural catheter
5. Urinary catheter
MAIN GOALS
- Pulmonary function improvement
- C.V.P. → 5-12 cm H2O
- AP → optimal
- CF → <100-120/ min
- Urine → 30-60ml/h
- Pain
- Antibiotics
Intra-OP- OP timing
- Emergency
→ but not too late and not too late
Strangulations
→ As early as possible!
Germs → endotoxins → catecholamine-like (MCRØ), DIC, mitochondrial block → DEATH
Intra-OP evaluation of intestinal viability
→ Very important (resect/ not resect?)
- Color
- Pulsations
- Bowel movements
- Intra-operatory bowel recovery
Short bowel syndrome
- Small bowel
- Limits (survival: 30-60cm; acceptable: 100-120cm)
Aggravating factors
- Ileum resection
- Right hemicolectomy associated
- Pervious gastric resection
→ Consequences
Jejuno-ileal insufficiency syndrome (Bennet-Hardwick)
- Intestinal alterations
- Malabsorption syndrome
→ Hypoproteinemia/ hypoalbuminemia
→ Anemia
→ Cachexia, vit. insufficiency
Post-OP

book.html:
Acute bowel obstructions

Doru Munteanu

DEFINITION:

The persistent pathological suppression of intestinal transit along with its loco-regional and general consequences on the whole body represents thecomplex multietiological clinical syndrome of acute bowel obstruction. Thus a more adequate and concentrated, yet not enough explicit variant is: permanent intestinal transit suppression (PITS).

CLASSIFICATION. ETIOLOGY:

Of the many variants of classification for bowel obstructions, the pathogenic ones, depending on the vascular disorders, have proved to be the most useful, as the prognosis of an acute bowel obstruction is decided in the first place by the presence or absence of intestinal ischemia. We already mention the importance of the topography of the obstruction, as “high” and “low” obstructions have different ways of expression, evolution and therapeutic peculiarities.

Fig.x: Upper, midd and low mechanical bowell obstructions

Nonmechanical/Paralytic ileus:

Dynamic intestinal motility disorders are rare; they occur at segmental level or over the entire length of the intestinal tract and are produced by exaggerated and prolonged spasms (tabetic colic, lead poisoning, porphyria). Bowel paresis (adynamic ileus) occurs more frequently. In these cases, the intestine becomes inefficient, inert, non-propulsive, in the absence of any mechanical obstruction, with intact intestinal vascularization.

A. Metabolic causes:

1. Severe acidosis (diabetes mellitus, “status asthmaticus”),

uremia, severe electrolyte imbalances (hypopotassemia, hyponatremia),

hypothyroidism, hypoproteinemia;

2. Severe anemias;

3. Abdominal (pelvic) irradiation;

4. Neurologic lesions: - epilepsy, brain tumors, multiple

sclerosis, colon pseudo-obstruction

B. Reflex causes:

1. Common postoperative bowel paresis

2. Mesenterial torsion / cavitary organs distension:

-acute fallopian tube torsion;

-reno-ureteral colic;

-biliary colic;

-acute urinary bladder distension;

3. Pleural/thoracic disorders (pneumonia, thoracic traumas, myocardial right ventricle infarction – bowel paresis associated with epigastric pain and shock ! - );

4. Retroperitoneal disorders (hematomas, acute pancreatitis, abcesses);

5. Sterile intraperitoneal fluid collections:

-acute onset of ascites in liver cyrrhosis;

-hemoperitoneum;

-chemical peritonitis;

C. Septic causes:

1. Localized/difuse purulent peritonitis;

2. Septic conditions adjacent to peritoneal serosa: (pelvic, retroperitoneal, properitoneal abcesses, etc.).

Mechanical obstruction:

It is due to factors that cause the complete or almost complete obstruction of the bowel lumen, without affecting, at least initially, the blood supply of the intestinal wall.

The lesions that cause obstruction can be classified into three main groups:

A. Extrinsic compressions:

1. Benign or malignant mesenteric, uterine, ovarian, hepatic,

retroperitoneal tumors (renal, adrenal, primitive retroperitoneal,

pancreatic tumors), adenopathies;

2. Viscero-visceral or viscero-parietal adhesions, omentum fixed

to the abdominal wall or to other organs (Meckel’s diverticulum,

appendix);

3. Intraperitoneal foreign bodies (compresses or kits left after

previous surgery – extremely rare - );

Fig.x: a.extrinsic compresion of rectum by voluminous ovarian cyst; b. by adesions;

B. Intramural lesions:

1. Congenital atresias and stenoses – pediatric surgery.

2. Dysfunctionalized loop;

3. Benign or malignant primitive or metastatic tumors;

4. Specific inflammatory stenoses, retractions (TB, CROHN) or

non-specific ones (cicatricial stenoses, postirradiation);

5. Intramural hematomas;

Fig.x: a, b. Crohn’s disease enteral, multiple (a) and single (b) stenoses, respectivelly. c. distal stenosing rectal tumor

C. Endoluminal obstructions:

1. Biliary large stones migrated through bilio-digestive fistulas

(biliary “ileus”);

2. Phytobezoars (difficult-to-digest cellulose-rich food bolus);

3. Trichobezoars (hair balls – in psychopaths);

4. Ascarid ball (less common in adults, more frequent in

children);

5. Accidental (tooth fragments, bones, wood, plastic, etc);

Foreign bodies that cross the digestive tract may become obstructive, particularly at the level of the narrow anatomical sites: pylorus, duodenal curvatures, ileo-cecal valve, the rectosigmoid flexure, and the anal canal.

Fig.x: endoluminal rare rectosigmoid junction impaction of migrated large biliary stone (cholecysto-colic fistula).

Bowel strangulations:

This category has an augmented severity score as it combines from the beginning the mechanical obstruction of the bowel (“double closed loop” , “one end”closed loop) with the interruption of venous drainage/arterial supply of the bowel wall and consecutive ischaemia, necrosis and perforation.

A.External strangulations:

1. External hernias

2. Strangulated incisional hernias

3. Eviscerations.

Fig.x: External strangulations. a. Giant strangulated right inguino-scrotal hernia; b. Giant strangulated umbilical hernia

B.Intraperitoneal strangulations:

1. Internal hernias

2. Invaginations (intussusceptions)

3. Volvulus (bowel torsion)

4. Ischemic adhesions.

These account for 25% of all cases of acute bowel obstruction; the internal strangulations have a dismal prognosis as usually their diagnosis is established late and bowel necrosis is frequent.

Fig.x: Internal strangulations: a. intussusception; b. volvulus (torsion)

Bowel infarctions:

By far the most severe variant, with the highest mortality !

Although the majority of handbooks, as well as the present manual, allocate a separate chapter to this condition, we may say that regardless of the size of the affected vascular axis or the extension of the ischemic intestinal segment, parietal infarction secondary to vascular obstruction is concomitant with aperistaltism, which justifies the inclusion of this entity in the category of intestinal occlusions.

The main event is in this case the suppression of the segmental or total blood supply of the intestinal tract, which results in hemorrhagic intestinal infarction (also severely infected from the beginning).

The causes of enteromesenteric infarction are:

1.Arterial trunk obstructions;

-emboli;

-thromboemboli.

2. Venous trunk obstruction (thrombosis);

3. Impairment of bowels’ wall microcirculation.

Fig.x: Extended small bowell infarction

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The important alterations of the body homeostasis induced by intestinal obstruction initially start at the level of the affected loop and of the intestinal tract upstream.

The most effective study model is that of the pathophysiology of the “simple” mechanical bowel obstruction (with no initial vascular involvement):

At the onset of the obstruction, its’ persistency represents a noxious stimulus that will trigger, due to increased intralumenal tension, the bowel response, which will attempt to overcome the obstruction by an increase in intestinal peristaltism and an excessive production of enteral glands’ secretion (Şuteu).

The pathological persistence of the obstruction will shortly result in the impairment of all functional regulation systems, the bowel being gradually overcome by the immutable, permanent obstruction so that the initial phase of peristaltic fight is followed by the energy exhaustion of the intestinal muscle fibers and the onset of distension through muscle atonia; consecutive endolumenal accumulation of fluids and gas occur; distension and accumulationsprogressively extend upstream of the obstacle, until the entire suprajacent digestive tract becomes a huge atonic reservoir containing enormous parasitic fluid and gas accumulations.

1. Intraluminal water-ion accumulations – result from the paroxysmal increase in fluids’ accumulations into the bowel lumen, combined with the progressive decrease and finally the suppression of absorption.

Fig.x: Bowell distension duet o continous acummulation of fluids and gas

The accumulated secretions coming from the digestive organs and bowel loops upstream, will continuously supply the newly created parasitic compartment with very rich in ions (Na+, K+, Cl-) fluids as follows: - saliva, 1000-1500ml/24h; - gastric juice, 1500-2500ml/24h; - biliary fluid, 10001200ml/24h; - pancreatic juice, 800-1200ml/24h; - enteral juice, 20003000ml/24h. Thus, between 6300ml and 9400ml of digestive fluids will be accumulated above the bowel obstruction; normally, these abovementioned fluids do participate in the complex physiologic processes of digestion and absorbtion, but in the end, after they have played their role, these fluids are reabsorbed, recuperated and reintroduced into the normal turnover of body’s physiology. The problem with the ABO is that there is no turnover anymore; the fluid’s displacement between the normal extra- and later, intracellular fluids’ compartments and the obstructed/distended bowels has a “one way” pattern, as these fluids are continuously “pumped” into the bowels, never to be recuperated again. The result will be a severely dehydrated organism and a paradoxically hyperhydrated bowel.

The lower the obstruction, the higher the accumulations above, which thus generate ahugely distended intestinal tract above the obstruction.

Thus, a pathological fluid space has been formed by an intestinal and intraperitoneal fluid-ion sequestrations, which constantly depletes the fundamental extra- and then intracellular water compartments; the so-called third parasitic fluids compartment has been created. It will cause a lifethreatening imbalance in the two physiological spaces; the critical loss of electrolytic fluids has been estimated at about 6.5 l (9% of the body weight), a volume that is easily reached and exceeded during the spontaneous evolution of the acute bowel obstruction.

2. Gas accumulations occur after the complete suppression of absorption, following the fluids’ accumulation; about 70% of the accumulated gas results from excessive swallowed air, the rest being the result of biochemical reactions and excessive digestive juices, as well as of excessive activity of the microbial flora.

As a direct consequence of this water and gas accumulations that result in a continuous increase of intestinal distension, intestinal (and intraabdominal) pressure increases (normal value 2-5 cm H O) and the bowel

2 wall is virtually squashed; thus, at values exceeding 10-15 cm H O, venous

2 circulation is closed (return pressure in venules – 15 cm H O); when pressure

2 within the obstructed loop exceeds 20cm H O, capillary collapse also occurs.

2 At pressures higher than 20-60 cm H O, which are reached in double closed

2 loops (volvulus, strangulations), arteriolar circulation is closed as well. As a consequence, with closure of venular circulation, the obstructed bowel exhausts continuously fluids and ions from the extracellular hydric compartment while absorption from the lumen is completely abolished. Thus,

the venularcollapse represents in fact the fundamental event that finally

closes the vicious circle and makes the process irreversible !

On the other hand, the impairment of capillary permeability determines diffusion of albumins in the interstitium, resulting in an extended bowel wall edema that supplementary contributes to the general water-ion depletion.

Ascites formation during acute bowel obstructions is common and represents another fraction of the third parasitic compartment.

Thus, all these fluid-ion losses sequestered in the huge parasitic reservoir are initially exclusively delivered by the extracellular water compartment; 12-24 hours later, intracellular water and potassium will be depleted as well, thus the final result will be a very severe general, extra- and intracellular, dehydration.

3. Acid-base imbalance

From the point of view of acid-base balance, patients with bowel obstruction will develop a mixed (metabolic and respiratory) acidosis.

Obstruction by strangulation

In this particular pathogenic type, vascular involvement is concomitant with the obstruction of the intestinal lumen. However, the direct consequences of ischemia will be the most important, as fluid-ion accumulations in distension can no longer fully manifest like in nonstrangulated obstructions.

Necrosis is the specific element of intestinal strangulation, being closely followed by infection and toxaemia, factors that rapidly lead to septico-toxic, rather than hypovolemic shock.

Two main variants are included in this category:

a) The variant of the obstructed ischemic loop in a single

area:

-rigid adhesion compressions;

-lateral incomplete stricture hernia (Richter type)

b)The variant of the acute double closed loop:

-internal/external hernia strangulation

-volvulus (torsion)

-invagination (intussusceptions).

Intra intestinal pressure in strangulations rapidly increases to values inducing the collapse of microcirculation and even arterioles (30-60 cm H O),

2 resulting in an intraparietal hemorrhage (blood infiltration) that after 6-12 hours becomes a hemorrhagic intestinal infarction.

The septic-toxic factor, characteristic of and decisive for the evolution of strangulated bowel obstruction, is derived from the bacterial intestinal population whose development is highly favored by distension, acute ischemia and stasis. The most feared germs from the point of view of exoand endotoxins’ production are the anaerobic gram negative ones (Clostridium perfringens, Welchii, bacteroides fragilis). Transparietal (mucoepitelial) penetration of these and their toxins with portal and lymphatic spread in the general circulation is due to the morphofunctional alteration of the mucous-epithelial barrier, early compromised by ischaemia.

Thus, occlusions by strangulation have a much more rapid and severe evolution. The fact that mortality reaches up to 15-20% in cases with irreversible bowel necrosis is significant.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Symptomatology

a) Pain. The following are typical particularly for mechanical

obstructions:

-colicy, intermitent pain;

-rapid increase in intensity, with a maximum of 30-60s, followed

by:

-a rapid and total decrease.

These three semiological features define the initial phase of “fight” of the obstructed bowel.

The free time interval between the colics has a particular clinical relevance:

  • For proximal jejunal obstructions, it is about 5 min, for the ileum 5-20

min, and for the colon more than 20 min.

-Strangulations and enteromesenteric infarctions have a permanent, high intensity pain; they cannot be controlled by pain killers.

-Rapid and complete volvulus has a brutal, syncopal onset, with the same continuous high intensity pain.

-Pain is initially located at the level of the obstruction and subsequently becomes generalized.

-In functional bowel pareses, pain is diffuse, continuous, of low-moderate intensity.

b) Vomiting is initially reflex, due to intraparietal tension at mesenteric level. Later, vomiting becomes productive, with regurgitation, also due to antiperistaltic waves, and during the late atonic phases of obstructed occlusion, vomitus is abundant, yet without effort, due to “overfullness”. However, this characteristically brings no relieve to the patient!

-In high, proximal obstructions, vomiting is early, repeated, persistent and highly unbalancing; patients vomit clear biliary fluid.

  • On the contrary, in low ileal obstructions, vomitus initial containes food

remains, then becomes bilious, later porraceous (turbid bile) and finally faeculent.

  • In low, distal (recto-sigmoid) obstructions, vomitingoccurs lateand is

less common.

The faeculent nature of vomitus is a sign of severe prognosis, being due not to the reflux of the colic content in the small bowel (an extremely rare phenomenon, when the ileo-cecal valve is overcome by intracolic high pressure), but to the abnormal overgrowth of excessive faecal bacteria at 2448 hours after the onset of the ileal obstruction.

c) The absence of fecal and gas transit is defining for the syndrome, but it has no absolute value. Thus, in high obstructions, the initial gas or even faecal emissions from the distal intestine is possible and may persist even for days, sometimes leading to a dangerous delay of diagnosis.

  • The subocclusive (König) syndrome is characteristic for the incomplete

obstructions of the small intestine and the ileocecal segment. This consists of colicy pain with a fixed point at the level of the obstruction, with the increase of meteorism, followed by hydro-aeric noises, borborigmi and finally diarrhea and gas debacle, resulting in the transient relief of the patient; similar episodes last for minutes and are recurrent.

Associated, sanguinolent-glaireous stoolsmay occur in some invaginations andin enteromesenteric infarction (late clinical sign – severe prognosis !).

Clinical signs can be grouped into abdominal signs, observed during abdominal examination (inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation), which should be associated with digital rectal examination, and extraabdominal or general signs.

A. Abdominal signs:

a) Inspection:

I. Meteorism does not appear immediately, yet it is oneof thecardinal signs that occur during the first 24 hours. A certain degree of abdominal distension is present in all forms of occlusion (except for high, proximal obstructions, also termed “with flat abdomen”). In functional, adynamic bowel pareses, distension is intense and diffuse, symmetrical yet painless.

Inmechanical obstructions of the distal ileum, distension is high, localized in the center of the abdomen.

In distal rectosigmoid obstructions, meteorism is also extensive, but localized in the flanks and epigastric.

In sigmoid volvulus, the “most extensive abdominal distension” occurs; the meteoristic balloon is huge, asymmetrical, ovoid, oriented from the left iliac fossa towards the right upper quadrant. A symptomatic triad has been adopted for this condition (the von Wahl triad), which consists of: enormous asymmetrical and mobile distension, elastic renitency and high tympanism.

The central and asymmetrical balloon (von Wahl sign) is considered as characteristic for small bowel volvulus.

Abdominal distension is absent in extremely high occlusions, in lateral stricture strangulations (Richter type hernias), as well as in the early phases of all bowel obstructions.

II. Visible peristaltism at the abdominal wall can be obviated in lean patients with mechanical obstruction, spontaneously or on abdominal percussion. Visible peristaltism with constant location and fixed point stop is characteristic of the König syndrome.

Abdominal inspection may also detect postoperative scars, as well as external hernias, incisional hernias which, although not included in the clinical picture of occlusion, are important for the orientation of preoperative etiological diagnosis.

b) Palpation. Right from the start, all potential of hernial sites have to be carefully examined. Palpation provides the following additional data:

-migrating tumor masses – in invaginations and faecalomas, or fixed tumor masses (stenosing tumors);

-inflamatory tumors;

-localized areas of tenderness and/or rigidity in ischaemic obstructions (strangulations, torsions, intussusceptions, infarctions). Once the perforation occured, diffuse abdominal rigidity, tenderness, fever and shock will dominate the clinical picture.

c) Percussion reveals tympanism that may cover hepatic dullness, in cases with important meteorism, or localized dullness in the case of loops filled with liquid. Dullness that can move to the flanks is due to ascites and signifies an advanced stage of occlusion.

d) Auscultation may detect hydro-aeric bowel sounds and borborygmi that occur concomitant with the colicky episode. In functional bowel pareses, “abdominal quiet” is perceived; yet, the same quiet abdomen is termed “death silence” in bowelinfarctions.

e) Rectal touch, a compulsory procedure, usually detects an empty rectal ampulla in untouchable obstruction (Hochwag sign). In orthostatism, a high rectal ampullary tumor can be detected. Obviously, low rectal neoplasms or impacted rectal faecalomas are easy to detect. Invaginated loops, possibly large sized bile stones migrated in the terminal ileon, can be detected as well.

B. Extra-abdominal signs

Initially, patient’s general condition is good, with normal pulse, no fever, patient only presenting anxiety, tachycardia during colicky episodes. Subsequently, the general condition progressively alters, and finally the occlusive septic-toxic shock occurs.

The general state which is affected from onset and is persistent appears in occlusions with initial vascular involvement.

The “tormented” facies by the ischemic colic is characteristic for strangulation.

Signs of general severe dehydration (thirst, dry tongue, hypotonic eye globes, persistent flaccid cutaneous fold) are associated with the decrease in diuresis (or even complete anuria – empty urinary bladder at initial catheterisation).

Fever strongly suggests an infected necrosis or a diffuse peritonitis which generates adynamic bowel paresis.

Marmoreal skin, hemodynamic collapse and hypothermia occur in the late, terminal phases of the septico-toxic shock.

CLINICAL VARIANTS:

1.Proximal small bowel obstructions are characterized by sudden onset, rapid evolution, with early, frequent, profuse vomiting. The rapidly and highly unbalancing fluid-ion losses are due to abundant vomiting rather than to the accumulations in the third hydric compartment and lead to hearly hypovolemic shock.

Abdominal distension is initially absent (“flat abdomen”). Gas and stools emissions are possible spontaneously or by enema, as the activity of bowels distal to the obstruction is preserved.

2. Distal ileal obstructions have a slower evolution. The third hydric compartment is extremely extensive. Vomiting occurs at later stages, but is abundant, turbid, later faeculent. Colicky episodes are less frequent, every 15-20 minutes, abdominal distension is symmetrical, central-abdominal. Dehydration occurs later but is severe.

3. Low (recto-sigmoid) obstructions have a long progressive, well tolerated evolution ove several days (4-7 days), with less intense colicky episodes, at longer time intervals (more than 20 minutes); vomiting can be absent or occur late. There is an important abdominal distension (flanks and epigastric, later generalized). Rectal digital examination can frequently detect the cause.

Peculiarities of colorectal obstructions: although fluid-air sequestrations progress slowly and their general effects occur at a late stage, it should be emphasized that the majority of obstructions at this level are malignant. Frequently these occlusions occur in aged patients, having multiple comorbidities.

a.Diastatic perforations predominantly occur in cases of obstructions with rectosigmoid location. Paradoxically, perforating lesions appear at a distance from the obstruction, namely at the level of the cecum. Due to the very high intralumenal pressure, the extremely distended cecum (“double closed loop”) might literally “explode”, generating a severe faecaliod diffuse peritonitis with very high mortality rates.

Fig.x: Distal recto-sigmoid tumoral obstruction with imminence of diastatic paradoxical cecal perforation

Lesions consist of peritoneo-muscular lacerations that can appear either as point perforations or longitudinal fissures, predominantly located at the level of the anterior cecal wall, which is less vascularized. Thus repeated abdominal X-ray examinations have to be done for the early detection of cecal distension close to or at dangerous values of 12-13cm (the so called “critical cecal diameter”), in order to prevent the imminent perforation (case in which immediate surgery is indicated).

b. Colic perforations, just above the obstructive tumor, even totally extended necrosis of the obstructed colon may occur as well.

4.The rotation (torsion) of a bowel loop by more than 180° with consecutive complete luminal obstruction (“double closed loop”), concomitant with the interruption of circulation (both venous and arterial) in the twisted mesentery is termed volvulus.

Fig.x: Volvulus (torsion); intraoperative view of bowell torsion around a enteroparietal adhesion

The clinical picture is alarming, with sudden onset, continuous (not intermittent-colicky !), very intense pain; vomiting is initially reflex (mesenteric torsion). Abdominal distension is central and symmetrical in jejunal volvulus, lower and asymmetrical, oriented from the left iliac fossa to the right upper quadrant in sigmoid volvulus. 90% of the latter occurs usually after 50 years of age, and are fulminant-acute forms, yet10% of the casesmaybe chronic intermittent forms.

Usually torsions are generated by full, heavy, long, mobile and hiperperistaltic loops (voluminous, cellulose-rich food bolus), with long mesenteries, whose posterior parietal insertion points are fixed and close to one another.

Mortality is as high as 10-15%; however, it can reach values up to 5070% once irreversible ischemia and necrosis have occurred.

4. Intestinal intussusceptions (invaginations), are frequent in children; they represent 0.5-1.5% ofacute bowel obstructions’ causes in adults.

Fig.x: Intussusception

Clinical manifestations are: sudden onset with typical intermittent colic, with longer periods of deceiving calm. Rectal bleeding occurs in 25% of the cases.

Although characteristic when detected, the “migrating tumor” can be detected by palpation only in 20% of cases. Metorism develops at a late stage. Vomiting is initially reflex. There are also chronic intermittent forms.

Intestinal invaginations consist of a telescoping bowel loop inside the next, distal one,resulting in three cylinders (intussusception); the intestinal segment that is telescoped (intussusceptum) forms the inner and middle walls, the outer wall belonging to the distal segment into which the telescoping takes place (intussuscipiens). During the physical exam, a tender mobile tumor is perceived. The mesentery being involved in the invagination, venous circulation (later the arterial one too !) is blocked. 48 hours later, the adhesions between the invaginated cylinders are already tight, making it irreversible, with consecutive ischemia and necrosis.

Intussusception is usually triggered by an inestinal tumor that is often pediculated (large polip) which, under the action of a hyperperistaltic wave, initiates the whole pathogenic sequence (adenomatous polyps, diverticula, foreign bodies).

(The triggering enteral tumors are mostly benign, while the majority of colic tumors are malignant !).

Intussusceptions can be: entero-enteral, ileo-colic, ileo-cecal, and colocolic.

5.Internal hernias. In these cases, the acute bowel obstruction syndrome is diagnosed preoperatively, yet it’s underlying cause remains to be established at laparatomy.

They consist of the entrapment, with or without strangulation, of mobile loops in orifices, recesses, or pouches within the peritoneal cavity. These real intraabdominal anatomical traps may be natural or congenital defects;they may occur secondary to abdominal-or thoracic trauma, or surgery as well. Thus internal hernias can be grouped into two main categories:

a) Internal hernias in preexisting orifices and fossettes:

-paraduodenal hernias;

-paracecal (Rieux) hernias;

-hernias through the foramen of Winslow (Treitz);

-congenital diaphragmatic hernias;

b) Internal hernias through traumatically or iatrogenically generated orifices;

-diaphragmatic

-transmesocolic (after gastrojejnostomies, Roux en Y loop, etc.)

-transmesenteric (retro-anastomotic after gastro-jejunal tube

placement).

Mortality rates are as high as 10-15%, even up to 40% once bowel necrosis occurs.

7. Strangulated external hernias:

The strangulated intestinal content of the hernia sack generates acute bowel obstruction (double closed loop) almost concomitantly with the initiating of its ischemic necrosis.

Clinical features are violent (abrupt onset of intense, continuous pain at the level of the strangulation, vomiting, pallor, sweating); examination promptly detects hernia strangulation, thus the diagnosis is established usually early. .

Femoral hernias are most frequently strangulated, but inguinal hernias are much more frequent.

Femoral hernias with lateral (incomplete) bowel strangulation are deceiving, as they do not cause intestinal occlusion, but on the contrary, they manifest by diarrhea (resulting in sometimes dangerous delay in diagnosis and treatment !).

8. Incisional hernias may generate acute bowel obstruction (with or without strangulation)by intrasaccular adhesions or at the level of the fibrotic hernial rings.

PARACLINICAL EXPLORATIONS

I.Radiological explorations:

a)Plain abdominal radioscopy/radiography is the most valuable exploration in acute intestinal obstructions.

The gas-fluid levels are the typical radiological diagnostic elements in bowel obstructions. They occur within 4-6 hours of the onset of occlusion.

-In a case of functional bowel paresis,the hydro-aeric images are uniformly distributed, from the level of the stomach to the small and large intestine (“chessboard” images).

-In small bowel obstructions, hydro-aeric images are numerous, localized in the central abdominal area, with a large transverse diameter.

-In distal colic occlusion, gas-fluid levels are less numerous, they outline the colic frame, having a large vertical diameter.

b)Irrigoscopy/irrigography is indicated only when the presence of a colic obstruction has been established or at least supposed to be highly probable, with a general state that does not require immediate emergency surgery.

Thus, in invaginations, a “trident-like” image can be obtained, which consists in stopping the contrast at a certain level, from where it is continued as two broad parallel bands over the length of another 10-15 cm. The “golf trouser” image is also found in invaginations.

Particularities:

1. In cases with volvulus of the sigmoid colon, the Frimann-Dahl sign was described, which consists of: a large volume, reversed U or omegashaped hydro-aeric image, which occupies the lower third of the abdomen, in which three opaque curves converging to the pelvis appear.

2. In “biliary ileus”, radiology detects, in addition to the typical gasfluid levels, the obstructive calculus as a radiopaque spot, located in upper pelvis or more frequently, in the right iliac fossa. Pneumobilia, as a consequence of the bilio-digestive fistula, can also be detected.

3. In acute bowel infarctions, intravascular gas images can be (rarely) detected, (superior mesenteric vein) outlining the portal tree in the right hypochondrium; gas infiltration in the necrotic bowel wall can be detected as well; both are generallysigns of dismal prognosis, signifying a irreversible ischaemia.

c) Abdominal ultrasound is one of the routine imagistic techniques, havig the great advantage of being completely non-invasive and largely available. It provides the surgeon with valuable data, allowing to determine the degree of distension of the loops, their wall thickness, the presence or absence of peristaltism, of fluid in the greater peritoneal cavity, as well as data on the etiology of the occlusive syndrome (pelvic-genital, pancreatic, retroperitoneal tumors, inflammatory blocks, septic intraperitoneal collections, aortomesenteric calcifications or various impacted foreign body.

d) Abdominal CTscan is the most valuable radiologic technique, as it enables the surgeon not only to confirm (or exclude) the acute bowel obstruction syndrome, but to establish the underlying cause as well.

e) Mesenteric angiography/Angio MRI, extremely useful although rarely used, can determine the site of vascular obstructions in intestinal ischemia. It has the great advantage of being rapid to perform, even in patients with an altered general condion.

II. Other techniques:

  • Endoscopy, less frequently practiced in emergency, can detect duodenal

obstructions within the range of the fibroscope (long enteroscopes are useful).

  • Laparoscopy is extremely useful for diagnostic and sometimes

therapeutic purposes, yet care must be taken in order to prevent iatrogenic bowel’s lesions due to sometimes important meteorism.

POSITIVE DIAGNOSIS:

Among all acute surgical abdomen entities, intestinal obstructions have a clinical features that individualizes them sufficiently, so that the diagnosis of syndrome does not pose special problems.

However, more important for the therapeutic approach is the preoperative determination of the presence of intestinal strangulation; the certainty or only the suspicion of a intestinal vascular involvement, requires immediate emergency surgery, not allowing a longer preoperative preparation as in the cases with “simple” nonvascular obstructions.

Thus, in strangulations, the clinical features are alarming and usually make the patients require medical assistance earlier. Onset is sudden, with acute continuous pain. Vomiting occurs early, abdominal distension, except for extensive volvulus, does not develop initially. The patient is anxious, pale, tachycardic, sweating and with a tendency to shock. The abdomen is painful on palpation and it may have localized muscle defense areas.

The radiological signs appear early, initially the distended horseshoe loop, subsequently the classical gas-fluids levels.

Fig.x: Corespondence between preoperative physical exam (meteorism), radiological exam (air/fluid levels) and intraoperative view (same case).

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS:

1. Chest trauma, pneumonia, basal pleurisy, right ventricle myocardial infarction can mimic the clinical features of bowel obstructions (reflex bowel pareses that do not requiresurgery). Careful clinical and radiological evaluation sorts out thecorrect diagnosis.

2. Acute adynamic bowel distension in severe, prolonged bronchial asthma episodes (“status astmaticus”) is characterized by continuous anal gas emission (not by failure to pass flatus !).

3. Acute gastric distension (usually postoperative) spectacularly subsides on the application of a nasogastric suction tube.

4. Acute ascites, rapidly occurring after hepatic portal decompensation, can mimic acute occlusive abdomen. Medical history, correct clinical examination and abdominal ultrasound allow to avoid surgery that would significantly aggravate the outcome of these patients.

5. Acute pancreatitis, (especially the so called “pseudo-obstructive” clinical variant), can determine inadequate surgery for edematous forms that can also improve under correct medical treatment. Abdominal ultrasound, CT and laboratory tests help make the diagnosis, thus avoiding a harmful laparatomy.

6. Painful subumbilical“tumor”generated by an important urinary bladder distention, in aged patients with obstructive prostate adenoma (causes sometimes a reflex bowel paresis) rapidly improves after the insertion of a urinary catheter.

7. Neglected diffuse peritonitis, particularly in non-reactive elderly (in which pain, abdominal tenderness, guarding and fever can be absent !), requires careful evaluation. In late stages just an important meteorism, vague abdominal pain and bowel paresis, may erroneously lead to aprolonged preoperative preparation, with severe consequences on peritoneal septicity.

8. Psychogenic distension in “ghost pregnancy” is clinically more difficult to differentiate from true obstructions, but the hysterical background, tachypnea with the chest maintained in an inspiratory position, 3-5 minutes of “blocked respiration” (in a plastic bag) may relieve the distension. In these patients, multiple previous unnecessary post-laparotomy scars are seen, which are due to repeated simulations (variants of Münchhausen syndrome).

The early making of diagnosis of the obstructive type of acute surgical abdomen is important, while the underlying cause remains to be established at laparatomy etiological.

Errors are particularly harmful in cases of false obstructive acute abdomen, in which inappropriate surgery is performed (on patients in whom laparotomy may aggravate the real disease- acute right ventricle myocardial infarction, acute hepatic/portal decompensation, etc.).

TREATMENT

There are four main therapeutic targets in the treatment of a case with acute bowel obstruction:

Restoration of water-ion and acid-base balance

To relieve the gastrointestinal distension

To deal with the cause of the enterocolic obstruction

To prevent future obstructive episodes

Treatig a case with acute bowel obstruction is no easy task. It requires a multidisciplinary, highly responsible and well coordinated team work (ICU specialist, lab, radiologist, internist) in which surgery alone – although of crucial importance – cannot be successful.

The first important therapeutic target, restoration ofhydric, electrolytic and acid-base balance is essential. The circulating fluid volume, together with the severely depleted/dehydrated and disballanced interstitial and intracellular water compartments, will be intensively and extensively restored throughout the entire duration of patient’s hospitalization, but the preoperative preparation is critical in order to stabilize the patient enough for a secure surgery.

It should be emphasized that the more advanced the evolution of a bowel obstruction, the longer the time period of preoperative re-equilibration. Thus, in occlusions with a moderately long evolution, after 3-6 hours of urgent repletion, the majority of patients become suitable for surgery, (after infusion of 2-4 l of saline with added sodium and potassium, according to plasma concentration of electrolytes). In long duration occlusions, with severe water-electrolyte imbalance and altered general state, this stage is extended to 12-24 hours (in non-ischemic variants). Fluids/ions replacement will continue during the operation and several days after.

Potential visceral failures are also treated during this stage (rapid digitalization, oxygen therapy, diabetic, diuretic compensation).

Large spectrum antibiotics are considered necessary, given that septicity increases with each hour of progression of an acute bowel obstruction, not to mention their special importance in malignant large bowels’ obstructions.

Alpha/beta blocking medication or preferably, a continuous epidural catheter, may contribute to the opening of intestinal wall microcirculation (and frequently, to the restoration of bowel movements) and control of pain.

Preoperative preparation requires a wide range of procedures in a relatively short time interval.

1. The placement of a naso-gastric suction tube, a duodenal tube or a intestinal Miller-Abbott tube, allows the evacuation of the gastrointestinal content, the suppression of vomiting, the relieving of intestinal distension, breaking the vicious circle between distension and intestinal wall ischemia; it fights the absorption of exo- and endotoxins, eliminates the danger of tracheal-bronchyc aspiration, allows the evaluation of fluid-ion losses, improves patient’s respiratory function and last but not least, emptying the stomach allows a secure induction of general anaesthesia.

2. The placement of two large peripheral venous catheters, and of a central venous catheter allows the constant monitoring of CVP (normal values 5-15cmH2O), a crucial parameter to be observed especially in aged patients with cardiac insufficiency – prevents excessive hemodynamic burden and acute pulmonary congestion -

3. Placing a urinary catheter is extremely useful for it allows a good evaluation of rehydration (monitoring of urinary output on a hourly basis – 30-60ml normal values -).

Fig.x: At ED: naso-gastric suction tube, uretheral catheter, peripheral and central venous catheters.

Surgical treatment has two major objectives:

-removal of the obstruction

-removal of the toxic intestinal content and peritoneal effusions.

a. The timing of operation is chosen depending on:

1. The pathophysiological variety of the obstruction (ischemic or nonischemic);

2. The duration of evolution, the level of the obstruction and, correlated with these, the severity of metabolic imbalances;

3. The coexistence of associated diseases.

Thus, immediate emergency surgery is indicated in the following cases:

-All types ofbowel strangulations;

-Acute colic obstructions, in which naso-gastric suction is not so effective, when the plain abdominal radiograph reveals that the“critical cecal diameter” has been reached (12-13 cm);

-All small bowel obstructions hospitalized before the onset of severe water-ion imbalances;

-Any occlusive variant that is certainly or probably ischemic.

The following can be delayed with a view to prolonged re-equilibration:

1. Cert mechanical nonischaemic obstruction, which has spontaneously evolved until the occurrance of water-ion imbalances that benefit from preoperative repletion.

2. Cases with exceptionally severe concomitant life-threatening visceral failures.

Choosing of the time for surgery ismade individually for each case.

Any failure of medical treatment requires surgery.

a. General anesthesia is the best option in these severe cases.

Extremely useful, particularly in the ischemic variants, is the epidural catheter; it offers great advantages, ensuring in addition to good analgesia a certain improvement in intestinal wall microcirculation and a more rapid resumption of postoperative bowel movements (splanchnic sympathicolysis). It also offers advantages in elderly patients with multiple deficiencies, with highly severe pulmonary failure, for whom orotracheal intubation poses risks.

In extreme cases, local anesthesia can be used for minimum surgical decompression (cecostomy).

b. The approach route will be median sub- and supra-umbilical laparotomy that allows a correct and complete surgical approach. In well selected cases, with only moderate meteorism, in which only limited adhesions are suspected, laparoscopic approach is a good option.

c. Surgical procedure depends on the cause of obstruction and the viability of the intestine.

If the loop is not viable, resection is compulsory with (or without) restoration of digestive tract continuity (termino-terminal, termino-lateral latero-terminal anastomoses; in patients withseverely altered performance index or doubtable quality of anstomotic partners, these aretransparietally externalized in a first stage - ostomies – and later, subsequent resection and transit restoration.

Criteria for the assessment of the viability of the loop:

If the intestinal loop has a doubtful appearance, with borderline viability, the mesentery will be infiltrated with novocain, the loop is enveloped in compresses impregnated with warm saline and is reintegrated into the abdomen on a trial basis, for 15-20 minutes, whileoptimal blood pressure values and oxygenation are ensured.

Subsequent evaluation ofbowel’s viability is based on the dynamics of three elements: the color of the loop, peristaltism, and arterial pulsations.

Normalization of the loop’s color (from dark cyanotic blue to normal pinkish), together withrestoration of mesenterial arteries’ pulsations, signify the restoration of blood supply, and are important yet not essential criteria. The crucial sign that allows the surgeon to responsably affirm the viability of the loop (and consequently to abstain from resection) is the resumption ofobvious peristaltic movements (signifying the morphological and functional integrityof the myenteric and Auerbach’s neuromuscular plexuses’ function).

The most reliable method is the use of fluxmeters based on the Doppler effect for the detection of signals of effective blood flow at the antimesenteric margin of the loop.

If any doubt persists after the aforementionedmeasures of “intraoperative bowel’s resuscitation”,resection is indicated.

If the loops are viable, the decompression of the digestive tract is initiated, with the evacuation of the toxic-septic content by:

-its “retrograde milking” up to the level of a naso-gastric or preferably naso-intestinal large suction tube;

-decompression of the distended colon by thick transanal Faucher tubes;

-decompression by the opening of the digestive tract significantly increases the rate of septic complications and is to be avoided unless no other modality is found.

The treatment of lesions is adapted as follows:

1. In small bowels’ obstructions, the following procedures are initiated: dividing of adhesions; if there areadherent organs that strangulate or obstruct the bowel (salpinx, appendix, Meckel’s diverticulum), they will be resected; devolvulation of the volvulated loop, disinvagination, release from internal/external hernias, enterotomy with the extraction of the calculus (or another foreign body) with consecutive enterorrhaphy (or enterostomy), excision of compressive tumors (uterine, mesenteric tumors), segmental resection in inflammatory or malignant stenoses.

2. In cases with iresectable obstructive tumors (or massive, impossibleto-dissect balls of extremely tight adherent loops), an internal by-pass (between the afferent and efferent loop) may be a good option (ileotransversostomy - in cecal, ascending colon or right flexure obstructive neoplasms - ; transverso-transversostomy - in mid transverse colon obstructions - ; transverso-sigmoidostomy - in splenic flexure malignant stenoses -). In other cases external diversions (permanent or temporary enterostomies, colostomies) are to be preferred.

In cases with obstructive, yet technically resectable tumors, good performance index, and not exaggerated bowels’dilations, the “all-inone”strategy is adopted. This means concomitant resection of the obstructing lesion together with the compromised bowel loop followed immediately by an anastomosis; it is the ideal variant, as it eliminates the cause of the obstruction, prevents a future obstruction and reconstructs the digestive tract, all in one single stage. Here are some examples: -- in case of an occlusive tumor of the ascending colon, a right hemicolectomy with ileotransversostomy is accomplished;

  • in resectable transverse colon tumors, a segmental resection of the

transverse colon with security margins, followed by termino-terminal colocolo-anastomosis is done;

  • in obstructive descending (or splenic flexure) colonic tumors, left

hemicolectomy followed by termino-terminal transverso-sigmoidostomy is performed;

  • in sigmoid stenotic tumors, the segmental sigmoid colonresection is

followed by termino-terminal colorectal anastomosis. or the Hartman procedure, which consists of the excision of the obstruction (the tumoral sigma) with the closure of the distal rectal stump and the externalization with terminal left iliac anus of the cranial colic stump, with the restoration of the digestive tract continuity in a second stage.

In patients with precarious general condition, even if technically feasible, resection is postponed and a simple external diversion is preferred as, do not forget, our main priority is to save the patient’s life first; this is performed by creation of a temporary colostomy above the obstruction, as a first step; radical resection can be accomplished 2-3 weeks later (second stage) with concomitant reconstruction (anastomosis) (second stage), or keeping the colostomy and reconstruct later (third stage).

Basically, there are four main types of ostomies: sigmoidostomy (for rectosigmoid obstructions), transversostomy (obstructions located from the rectum up to the left third of the transvers colon), cecostomy (rarely indicated nowadays, yet still useful in cases with imminence of paradoxical diastatic caecal perforation - complete neglected recto-sigmoid malignant obstruction in patients with severe comorbidities/poor general condition - ) and ileostomy (obstructions located upstream, on the small bowel.

As a rule all the abovementioned ostomies ca be temporary or permanent (choice depends again on local, technical tactical strategical and general criteria which will not be detailed here.

All the numerous strategical, tactical and technical variants are selected and adopted by the surgeon after a rigorous evaluation of technical (local extension of tumors, loco-regional anatomical alterations generated by the obstruction, anatomical individual particularities of the patient, etc.), general (age, patients’ performance index, associated comorbidities, patients’ compliance – some never accept a colostomy ! -), and pathophysiological criteria ( duration from onset to admittance, intensity of metablic desorders , vascular involvement, etc.).

Postoperative treatment consists of:

1. The maintenance of the suction catheter until the resumption of digestive transit, which allows the breaking of the vicious circle of distension, protects digestive anastomoses, reduces abdominal tension at the level of the wound, prevents postoperative vomiting;

2. Volemic, ion and acid-base re-equilibration is continued;

3. Antibiotherapy;

4. Symptomatic treatment.

The treatment of functional occlusions is aimed in the first place at their causes, i.e. metabolic imbalances in dynamic occlusions are corrected.

In reflex functional occlusions, effective analgesia and the suppression of various colics (renal, biliary), the correct treatment of thoraco-pleuropulmonary disorders lead to the remission of occlusion.

In addition to these measures, nasogastric suction and the restoration of water-electrolyte balance are compulsory.

In alarming postoperative intestinal paresis, which tends to last more than 72 hours, an extremely beneficial solution is continuous peridural infiltration, which may have spectacular effects for the reasons mentioned above.

The great majority of dynamic occlusions are solved by the mentioned conservative measures.

When intestinal transit is not restored by these measures, surgery should be considered; the early reintervention can evidence a mechanical obstruction by early fibrinous adhesions, in which case early postoperative paresis has developed into a mechanical occlusion whose cause should be solved (Şuteu).

In paraseptic functional occlusions, the treatment of the cause, of the septic focus generating intestinal paresis is compulsory, which requires surgery. Thus, the correct treatment of peritonitis of various etiologies is the therapeutic solution for the accompanying dynamic occlusion. The drainage of pelvisubperitoneal, pre- and retroperitoneal foci also leads to the elimination of the occlusion. In cases with large distension, transient enteroor colostomies may become necessary.

COMPLICATIONS

Acute bowel obstruction is a complex syndrome, which in fact is itself a complication in the evolution of causative disorders. Particular complications generatedby bowel obstructions can be grouped into three large categories: a. Complications resulting from it’s spontaneous, untreated, development:

  • Various bowel necroses, diastatic caecal perforations – in neglected cases;
  • Diffuse/localized peritonitis; -Septico-toxic shock with multiple organ failures

b. Pre- and intraoperative complications:

-Gastric/intestinal content lung aspiration – the most severe

bronchopneumonia

-Bowel perforations with peritoneal contamination c. Postoperative complications:

  • Eviscerations

-The critical ARDS lung; -Acute cardiac, respiratory, renal, hepatic failures; -Acute stress digestive lesions (UDH); -Pulmonary thrombembolism; -Acute gastric dilation.

  • Anastomotic break-down, fistulae, abdominal abcesses, peritonitis,

sepsis

  • Multiple recurrent obstructive episodes;

-Blind loop syndrome (as a consequence of internal diversions that exclude large, extended bowel segments);

  • Short bowel syndrome (after extreme extended bowel resections
